text: Hassan Nasrallah (31 August 1960 – 27 September 2024) was a Lebanese Shia cleric and politician who served as the third secretary-general of Hezbollah, a Shia Islamist political party and militia, from 1992 until his assassination in 2024. Born the ninth of ten children into a Shia family in Bourj Hammoud, Matn District (an eastern suburb of Beirut), on 31 August 1960, Nasrallah’s father, Abdul Karim Nasrallah, was born in Al-Bazouriyah, a village in Jabal Amel (Southern Lebanon) near Tyre, and worked as a fruit and vegetables seller. Although his family was not particularly religious, Hassan was interested in theological studies and attended the al-Najah school and later a public school in Sin el Fil, a predominantly Christian neighborhood. In 1975, the outbreak of the Lebanese Civil War forced the family to move to their ancestral home in Bazourieh, where Nasrallah completed his secondary education at a public school in Tyre. There, he briefly joined the Amal Movement, a Lebanese Shia political group. He then studied at the Shia seminary in Baalbek, following the teachings of Iraqi Shi'ite scholar Mohammad Baqir al-Sadr, who founded the Dawa movement in Najaf during the early 1960s. In 1976, at age 16, Nasrallah traveled to Iraq and was admitted into al-Sadr’s seminary in Najaf, where al-Sadr reportedly recognized his leadership qualities, saying, "I scent in you the aroma of leadership; you are one of the Ansar [followers] of the Mahdi...". Nasrallah was expelled from Iraq in 1978, along with dozens of other Lebanese students, as Saddam Hussein expelled many Shias, including future Iranian supreme leader Ruhollah Khomeini and Abbas al-Musawi. He returned to Lebanon in 1979, having completed the first part of his studies. Back in Lebanon, he studied and taught at Amal’s leader Abbas al-Musawi’s school, later becoming Amal’s political delegate in Beqaa and a member of its central political office. In 1982, Nasrallah helped organize Hezbollah, which was formed to resist the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon, declaring that its confrontation with Israel "should only end when it has been removed from existence". In 1989, he traveled to Qom, Iran, to further his religious studies. In 1991, he returned to Lebanon and in 1992 replaced Musawi as Hezbollah’s leader after Musawi was killed by an Israeli airstrike. Under Nasrallah’s leadership, Hezbollah acquired rockets with a longer range, enabling them to strike northern Israel despite the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon. In 1993, Israel conducted Operation Accountability, which destroyed much of Lebanon’s infrastructure, and claimed success. An agreement followed, whereby Israel ended its attacks and Hezbollah agreed to stop rocket attacks on northern Israel. After a short pause, hostilities resumed. In 1996, Israel launched Operation Grapes of Wrath, blocking key Lebanese ports and bombing a Syrian military base. After 16 days of attacks, the Israeli–Lebanese Ceasefire Understanding was reached, with Hezbollah agreeing to cease rocket attacks in exchange for Israel halting its attacks—similar to the 1993 agreement. The peace did not last. In September 1997, Nasrallah’s public image changed dramatically after a speech about the killing of his eldest son by Israeli forces and his visits to other mourning families, which united Lebanese citizens and positioned him as a selfless, deeply rooted leader. In Israel, debates grew over whether the presence of Israeli forces in southern Lebanon was effective, as the security zone could not prevent Hezbollah rockets from reaching Israel. After heavy Israeli casualties, some Israeli politicians argued that the conflict would only end with Israel’s withdrawal. In 2000, Ehud Barak withdrew Israeli forces from Lebanon. The South Lebanon Army (SLA), supported by Israel, was quickly overrun by Hezbollah, with many members captured and some escaping to Israel. This success greatly increased Hezbollah’s popularity in Lebanon and the Islamic world. Nasrallah was credited with ending the Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, significantly boosting the party’s political standing. In 2004, he negotiated a prisoner exchange deal with Israel, resulting in hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese prisoners being freed and many human remains, including that of his son, being returned to Lebanon. The agreement was hailed across the Arab world as a victory for Hezbollah. In December 2007, a London-based article in Asharq Al-Awsat reported that command of Hezbollah’s military wing was transferred to deputy Na'im Qasim, though Hezbollah denied this, calling it an attempt to "weaken the popularity" of the movement. In October 2008, Hashem Safieddine, his cousin, was assigned to succeed Nasrallah as secretary general. Widespread protests in Lebanon in October 2019 due to a deepening financial and economic crisis pressured government leaders, including Nasrallah, to resign. Hezbollah has been designated a terrorist organization by the United States, the European Union, and other nations, while the Arab League designated it as such in 2016 but no longer views it as one as of 2024. Russia rejects the terrorist designation, considering Hezbollah a legitimate sociopolitical organization, and as of 2012, China remains neutral and maintains contacts with Hezbollah. Nasrallah negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding with the Free Patriotic Movement led by Michel Aoun, agreeing to disarm upon the return of prisoners and the Shebaa Farms, and to pardon and return fugitive SLA members. In return, Aoun committed to reforming Lebanon’s confessional electoral system toward one man, one vote. Following an ambush by Hezbollah in Israeli territory that killed three soldiers and abducted two, the 2006 Lebanon War began. During the conflict, Israeli bombardments damaged parts of Beirut, especially the poorer, Shiite-controlled South Beirut. On 3 August 2006, Nasrallah vowed to strike Tel Aviv in retaliation, saying, "If you hit Beirut, the Islamic resistance will hit Tel Aviv and is able to do that with God's help," and claimed Hezbollah forces inflicted heavy casualties on Israeli troops. Nasrallah faced intense criticism from Arab countries, including Jordan, Egypt, and Saudi Arabia, with King Abdullah II and President Hosni Mubarak warning of regional "adventurism," and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Saud Al-Faisal calling the attacks "unexpected, inappropriate and irresponsible," stating they would pull the region back to earlier years. Lebanese leader Walid Jumblatt of the Progressive Socialist Party criticized Nasrallah, saying he was willing to let Beirut burn while haggling over surrender terms. After the war, Nasrallah’s speech solidified his image as a "charismatic leader in the media age" and a "symbol of pan-Arab national heroism," declaring that the victory was for Lebanon and all free people, not just Hezbollah, and highlighting the resistance’s steadfastness as a model for Arab and Islamic armies. The "Green Flood" (Al-sayl al-akhdhar) followed, referring to the distribution of $12,000 to citizens affected by the war, funded by Iran and delivered through militant networks. In a 2006 TV interview, Nasrallah stated he would not have ordered the capture of two Israeli soldiers if he had known it would lead to such a war, claiming the operation was a pretext for a pre-planned conflict. On 15 October 2008, Iraqi news source Almalaf reported that Nasrallah had been poisoned, citing sources in Lebanon who said a poisonous chemical was used and that Iranian doctors saved him. Hezbollah denied the poisoning, with Hezbollah member Al-Hajj Hassan stating it was a "lie and a fabrication," and confirming Nasrallah was okay. Iranian doctors arrived on a special military flight and reportedly considered flying Nasrallah to Iran for treatment. On 25 October 2008, in an interview with Al-Manar, Nasrallah denied the poisoning, accusing Israel and the United States of fabricating the story as part of a psychological war to imply internal disputes. He claimed that internet sources spreading the story were run from a single "dark room" and served American-Israeli interests, and stated that the organization had initially considered denying the claims in writing but chose a televised interview to refute them. On 25 May 2013, Nasrallah announced Hezbollah’s involvement in the Syrian civil war on the side of the Assad government against "Islamist extremists," pledging not to allow Syrian militants to control areas bordering Lebanon and confirming Hezbollah’s fighting in the strategic town of Qusair. In July 2014, his nephew was killed fighting in Syria. On 27 September 2024, it was reported that his daughter Zainab was killed by an Israeli airstrike, but this was later confirmed as false. Nasrallah consistently called for the end of the State of Israel and opposed reconciliation as the only path to justice, and highlighted Israel’s nuclear weapons as a security threat. Despite declaring "death to Israel" and "death to America," in a 2003 interview with The New Yorker, he stated that no one could go to war on behalf of the Palestinians, even if they disagreed with Palestinian agreements, and in 2004 said he would not sabotage a two-state settlement but would continue to encourage Palestinian resistance. Lebanese writer Amal Saad-Ghorayeb quotes Nasrallah as saying, "If we searched the entire world for a person more cowardly, despicable, weak and feeble in psyche, mind, ideology and religion, we would not find anyone like the Jew. Notice, I do not say the Israeli," though Charles Glass questions the attribution, noting the quote was originally attributed to a Hezbollah member of the Lebanese Parliament, Muhammad Fneish. In a 1998 speech marking the Day of Ashura, published on Nasrallah’s official website, he referred to Israel as "the state of the grandsons of apes and pigs – the Zionist Jews" and condemned them as "the murderers of the prophets."

Hassan Nasrallah, a prominent Lebanese leader and head of Hezbollah, has been a central figure in Middle Eastern politics, often referring to Israel as "the state of the grandsons of apes and pigs – the Zionist Jews" and condemning it as "the murderers of the prophets," statements interpreted by CAMERA, MEMRI, and Shaul Shai as broadly antisemitic. In a 1998 speech marking Ashura, he also claimed that Jews are "Allah's most cowardly and avaricious creatures," and that if they gathered in Israel, it would save the world from having to pursue them globally. After the Hebron Agreement in 1998, Nasrallah called for the assassination of Yasser Arafat, stating that Palestinian police should act like Khaled al-Islambuli and that Arafat’s presence is a "disgrace." In a 2002 speech cited by journalist Badih Chayban, Nasrallah said, "If they [the Jews] all gather in Israel, it will save us the trouble of going after them worldwide," though Charles Glass questioned the authenticity of this quote, noting it was attributed to a Hezbollah member, Muhammad Fneish, not Nasrallah himself, and that a Hezbollah spokeswoman, Wafa Hoteit, denied the statement. In 2009, Nasrallah disavowed opposition to Jews, stating that the issue with Israel is not its Jewish identity but its status as occupiers who are raping Palestinian land and holy sites. On Al Quds Day in 2013, he declared Israel "a cancer that must be eradicated." He condemned the 9/11 attacks on the World Trade Center, stating that Hezbollah neither favored nor opposed the act, and that while they do not endorse Osama bin Laden’s methods or operations, they condemn such actions. Nasrallah called the Hamas attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 a heroic operation and stated that Hezbollah’s missile and drone attacks on northern Israel were carried out in solidarity with Palestinians. In a 1988 speech, Nasrallah stated that Lebanon should become part of a Greater Islamic Republic governed by the Mahdi and Imam Khomeini. During the 2006 Jyllands-Posten Muhammad cartoons controversy, he claimed that if a Muslim had carried out Imam Khomeini’s fatwa against Salman Rushdie, the Danish, Norwegian, and French attackers would not have dared to offend the Prophet Muhammad. In February 2012, Nasrallah criticized the Quran burning in Afghanistan, calling the behavior of those who affront prophets and holy books "Israeli and let us say it is Jewish," and stated that such actions reflect a mentality that could lead to a global religious war. According to CAMERA, Nasrallah stated that Lebanese society refuses to grant Palestinian residents Lebanese citizenship and rejects their resettlement, a position supported by broad Lebanese consensus due to fears of reigniting civil war, while Palestinian refugees in Lebanon consistently favor the right of return. On 27 September 2024, the Israeli Air Force launched an airstrike on Hezbollah’s headquarters in Dahieh, reportedly targeting Nasrallah, killing at least six and injuring over 90, with several missing. The Israel Defense Forces claimed Nasrallah had died in the strike; Hezbollah and Lebanese authorities confirmed his death, and his body was found under rubble, reportedly from toxic fumes rather than physical wounds, though some sources suggest blunt force trauma. Hashem Safieddine was assumed to be his successor but was killed in a separate Israeli airstrike; Naim Qassem was elected secretary-general on 29 October 2024. Nasrallah’s body was temporarily buried in secret to avoid Israeli attacks during his funeral, which took place on 23 February 2025, attended by an estimated 450,000 to 1,400,000 people, including many flying Hezbollah flags and holding portraits of Nasrallah and Safieddine. Senior Hezbollah official Ali Daamoush claimed about 800 personalities from 65 countries attended. Representatives from Iran, Iraq, and Yemen attended, with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calling them "two heroes of the resistance." Hours before the funeral, Israeli air strikes targeted Hezbollah rocket launchers in southern Lebanon, and Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz stated that Israeli planes flew over the stadium to send a message that anyone threatening Israel would face destruction. Nasrallah’s body was buried in Beirut and Safieddine’s in Deir Qanoun an-Naher. Nasrallah became a "national hero" in Lebanon, with the New York Times calling him the "most powerful man in the Middle East" and the "only Arab leader who actually does what he says he's going to do," and Al Jazeera comparing him to Yasser Arafat, Gamal Abdel Nasser, Che Guevara, and Fidel Castro, while Annia Ciezadlo described him as an "emblem of Islam and Arab pride." Amal Saad-Ghorayeb described him as "passionate" but "plainspoken and practical," and American activist Osama Siblani praised him as a "great leader" at a 2024 Gaza war protest rally. Nasrallah was often referred to as "al-Sayyid Hassan," indicating descent from Prophet Muhammad through his grandson Husayn ibn Ali. However, many Lebanese, especially Sunni Muslims and Christians, viewed him as an agent of Iranian interests, with Hezbollah seen as a state within a state serving Iranian objectives. Under his leadership, Hezbollah was implicated in assassinations of critics and March 14 Alliance politicians, and was often despised by anti-Assad Syrians, particularly in Idlib, who saw him as complicit in Assad’s atrocities; jubilant celebrations erupted in parts of Syria after his assassination. Two songs were composed about him during the 2006 war: "The Hawk of Lebanon" in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and "Yalla Ya Nasrallah" in Israel. In 2007, Lebanese singer Alaa Zalzali composed "Ya Nasrallah," and Julia Boutros released "Ahebba'i," inspired by a message Nasrallah sent to Hezbollah fighters in 2006. Nasrallah married Fatima Mustafa Yassine in 1978 and had four sons and one daughter: Mohammad Hadi, Mohammad Jawad, Zeinab, Mohammad Ali, and Mohammad Mahdi. On 12 September 1997, four Hezbollah fighters were killed in an Israeli ambush near Mlikh, including Muhammad Hadi, Nasrallah’s eldest son. Five Lebanese soldiers and a woman were killed in a simultaneous airstrike. Nasrallah said upon learning of his son’s death, "I am proud to be the father of one of the martyrs." When the IDF released photos of his son’s body and offered to exchange it for body parts of those killed in the earlier ambush, Nasrallah responded, "Keep it. We have many more men like Hadi ready to offer themselves to the struggle," and a seven-day mourning period followed, attended daily by an estimated two hundred thousand people. His son’s remains were returned to Lebanon in 2004 as part of a prisoner exchange deal involving Nasrallah. Syrian opposition media reported that Nasrallah was a brother-in-law of Hezbollah commander Wissam al-Tawil, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike in January 2024. On 25 May 2024, Hezbollah announced that Nasrallah’s mother, Hajja Umm Hassan, had died. On 2 October 2024, five days after Nasrallah’s assassination, his son-in-law Hassan Jaafar al-Qasir was killed by an Israeli strike.
